title: AI Financing Stress Culminates in a Midterm-Triggered Global Tech Rout
content:
AI anxiety hardened over the window from a valuation debate into a question about who funds the buildout. Neocloud distress was the tell: CoreWeave's credit-default swaps spiked to records, hyperscaler CDS on Meta, Nvidia and Oracle hit all-time highs, and much of this year's data-centre debt priced as junk, putting **circular financing** at the centre of the worry.

The stress crystallised after the 3 November midterms handed Democrats Congress, raising fears of data-centre moratoria and tighter AI oversight. The S&P 500 fell **4.4%** on 5 November — its worst session since April 2025 — the Nasdaq slid into correction and **$2.5tn** of value vanished in a day, with Asian tech following as Korea's Kospi dropped **5.3%**.

The rout spanned equities, credit and rates, handing government bonds a safe-haven bid; an Nvidia-led bounce on 6 November trimmed the weekly loss. Funding conditions and **neocloud** credit stay the swing factor into year-end.

title: Sticky Inflation Keeps the Fed Restrictive With a December Hike in Play
content:
The higher-for-longer regime stayed the macro backbone. Having lifted rates in September for the first time since 2023, the Fed held the funds target at **3.75%-4.00%** on 28 October in a split 10-2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favour of a further increase as the statement again called inflation elevated.

The data kept the hawks engaged. Headline PCE ran at **3.6%** year-on-year with core near 3%, and CPI firmed to **3.7%**, leaving little sign of last-mile progress. An economist consensus coalesced around a December move, with the 9 December decision and the 10 November CPI framed as the next catalysts.

The theme mattered because elevated discount rates pressured the richest equities and amplified the tech unwind, while keeping the **term premium** alive in the long end. The December decision and incoming inflation prints remain the pivotal swing factors into year-end.

title: Middle East De-escalation Unwinds the Energy Risk Premium
content:
After months in which the Iran war and a constrained Strait of Hormuz had kept crude elevated, the window's defining energy move was the unwind. Hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough and ceasefire talk pulled Brent sharply lower, erasing much of the earlier war premium even as the strait stayed below pre-war throughput.

The repricing was swift: Brent fell roughly **12%** on the week to around **$98**, retreating from six-month highs, with the slide extending as midterm results dented risk appetite and demand expectations. Sticking points over Iran's nuclear programme and the naval blockade left the de-escalation incomplete.

The move mattered beyond energy because cheaper crude eased one of the hotter inputs behind the inflation story, trimming a key upside tail for CPI just as the Fed weighed December. A durable reopening of Hormuz would deflate the **risk premium** further; renewed escalation remains the obvious tail risk.
